title: Programming Foundations
summary: The seven primitives every Kadi rule builds on: variables, operators, conditionals, loops, functions, arrays, dictionaries, and classes.

lessons.title: Variables and Types
lessons.bodyMarkdown:
# Variables in GDScript

A **variable** is a named slot that holds a value. In GDScript 4.3 you declare one with `var` and you should annotate its type so the editor catches mistakes the moment you type them.

A Kadi card has a **rank** (2 through Ace) and a **suit** (Hearts, Diamonds, Clubs, Spades). We model those directly:

```gdscript
var rank: int = 7
var suit: String = "Hearts"
var is_penalty: bool = false
```

Use `const` for values that never change — the four suits, the maximum hand size, the penalty value of a 3. Constants document intent and let Godot inline them.

GDScript is dynamically typed at runtime but statically checked wherever you annotate. Mixing them up — assigning a String to an int — throws a runtime error instead of silently corrupting your turn state.

> [!WHY]
> Type annotations convert an entire class of bugs ("I passed a String where an int was expected") into compile-time errors. In a turn-based game, a single bad cast mid-tournament can freeze the round — annotations make that impossible.

Variables carry Kadi's per-turn state: whose turn it is, the current penalty stack, the top card on the discard pile. Get the types right and the rules fall out naturally.

codeSnippets.code:
var rank: int = 7
var suit: String = "Hearts"
var is_penalty: bool = false
const MAX_HAND_SIZE: int = 5

func describe() -> String:
    return "Card: %d of %s" % [rank, suit]
codeSnippets.caption: Declaring typed variables and a constant for a Kadi card.

practicePrompt.instructions: Declare a typed variable `top_card_rank` set to 14 (Ace) and a boolean `can_play` set to true.
practicePrompt.solutionCode:
var top_card_rank: int = 14
var can_play: bool = true

quizQuestions.prompt: Which keyword declares a value that cannot change after initialization?
quizQuestions.explanation: `const` binds a name to a value at compile time and forbids reassignment, perfect for fixed game constants like MAX_HAND_SIZE.

quizQuestions.prompt: What happens if you assign a String to a variable annotated `: int`?
choices: It throws a runtime type error
quizQuestions.explanation: GDScript checks annotated types at runtime; assigning an incompatible type raises an error rather than corrupting state.

lessons.title: Operators and Booleans
lessons.bodyMarkdown:
# Operators and Booleans

A **boolean** is a value that is either `true` or `false`. Booleans are the glue of every rule in Kadi: "is this card playable?", "is the player out of cards?", "is the penalty stack empty?"

GDScript gives you the comparison operators `==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` and the logical operators `and`, `or`, `not`. They short-circuit: `and` stops at the first `false`, `or` stops at the first `true`.

```gdscript
var same_suit: bool = card.suit == top.suit
var same_rank: bool = card.rank == top.rank
var playable: bool = same_suit or same_rank
var is_penalty: bool = card.rank == 2 or card.rank == 3
```

Kadi leans heavily on `or`: a card is playable when it matches the suit **or** the rank of the top card. Use `and` only when both conditions must hold, like "is it a penalty card AND the stack is non-empty".

> [!WHY]
> Choosing `and` versus `or` is the most common logic bug in card games. `and` requires both conditions; `or` requires either. A playable-card check written with `and` would let almost nothing through, freezing the game — so we read each rule out loud before coding it.

Parenthesise compound expressions even when precedence would save you; readers should not have to recall operator tables.

codeSnippets.code:
func is_playable(card: Dictionary, top: Dictionary) -> bool:
    var same_suit: bool = card["suit"] == top["suit"]
    var same_rank: bool = card["rank"] == top["rank"]
    return same_suit or same_rank
codeSnippets.caption: Playable check uses `or` — match suit OR rank.

practicePrompt.instructions: Write a boolean expression `is_face_card` that is true when `rank` is 11 (Jack), 12 (Queen), 13 (King), or 14 (Ace).
practicePrompt.solutionCode: var is_face_card: bool = rank == 11 or rank == 12 or rank == 13 or rank == 14

quizQuestions.prompt: In Kadi, a card is playable if it shares the suit OR the rank of the top card. Which operator should the check use?
quizQuestions.explanation: Either condition is sufficient, so `or` is correct. `and` would require both to match, which only the identical card satisfies.

quizQuestions.prompt: What does `not (a or b)` evaluate to when a is true and b is false?
quizQuestions.explanation: `a or b` is true, and `not true` is false. De Morgan's laws are worth memorising for rule inversions.

lessons.title: Conditionals: if / elif / else
lessons.bodyMarkdown:
# Conditionals

A **conditional** lets your code branch. GDScript uses `if`, `elif`, and `else`. Indentation defines the block — four spaces, no tabs.

Kadi's penalty rules are a perfect fit. When the top card is a penalty card, the next player must either pick up the stack or play a counter-penalty:

```gdscript
if card.rank == 2:
    penalty += 2
elif card.rank == 3:
    penalty += 3
elif card.rank == Ranks.JOKER:
    penalty += 5
else:
    penalty = 0
```

Order matters: `elif` checks run only if previous `if`/`elif` were false. Put the most specific case first.

Godot 4 also offers `match` (covered in Phase 4) for switching on a single value with many branches. Prefer `match` when you compare one expression against several constants; prefer `if/elif` when each test is a distinct boolean.

> [!WHY]
> Branching is where rules live. By isolating each card's effect in its own `elif`, you make adding a new card a one-line change — no risk of accidentally altering the logic for existing cards. Flat branches keep the rules table-readable.

Always include an `else` for unexpected input during development so silent failures become loud crashes.

codeSnippets.caption: Branching on rank to compute penalty.

practicePrompt.instructions: Write a function `is_jump_card(rank)` returning true for Jack (11) and false otherwise, using a single if/else.

choices: Only if all previous if/elif were false and its condition is true
Only if the if was true
quizQuestions.explanation: `elif` is short for 'else if' — it runs only when earlier branches failed AND its own test passes.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why put the most specific case first in an if/elif chain?
choices: So general cases do not shadow specific ones
It is required by the compiler
quizQuestions.explanation: Earlier true branches win; a general test first would intercept specific cases that should run instead.

lessons.title: Loops: for and while
lessons.bodyMarkdown:
# Loops

A **loop** repeats a block of code. `for` iterates over a known range or collection; `while` repeats until a condition becomes false.

Dealing 4 cards to each of 4 players is a classic nested `for` (Kadi deals 3 or 4 cards depending on how many players sit down):

```gdscript
for player in range(4):
    for _ in range(4):
        hands[player].append(deck.pop_back())
```

Use `while` when you cannot predict the count — drawing until the deck runs out, or cascading jump cards until none remain.

```gdscript
while deck.size() > 0 and not has_match(hand, top):
    hand.append(deck.pop_back())
```

Every `while` loop must have a guaranteed exit. If the body never makes the condition false, you get an infinite loop and the game freezes.

> [!WHY]
> `for` loops over `range()` are bounded by construction — they always terminate. `while` loops require you to prove the condition will eventually fail. In Kadi, jump-card cascades use `while` because the chain length depends on what players hold, but you must cap iterations to avoid a stuck game.

Prefer `for` whenever the count is computable up front; reach for `while` only when termination is data-driven.

codeSnippets.caption: Nested for loops deal 4 cards to each of 4 players.

practicePrompt.instructions: Write a `while` loop that pops cards from `deck` into `hand` until `deck` is empty.

quizQuestions.prompt: Which loop is safest when the iteration count is known in advance?
quizQuestions.explanation: `for` over a bounded range cannot run forever — termination is guaranteed by the range itself.

quizQuestions.prompt: What MUST every `while` loop guarantee to avoid freezing the game?
choices: That the condition eventually becomes false
quizQuestions.explanation: Without guaranteed termination, the loop spins forever and the game hangs. Always verify the body advances toward the exit condition.

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.bodyMarkdown:
# Functions

A **function** is a named, reusable block of code. Declare it with `func`, optionally annotate parameters and return type, and `return` a value.

```gdscript
func can_play(card: Dictionary, top: Dictionary) -> bool:
    return card["suit"] == top["suit"] or card["rank"] == top["rank"]
```

Functions are the smallest unit of testable behaviour. Keep them short — under 20 lines when you can — and give them one job. A function called `apply_penalty` should adjust the penalty stack and nothing else; reporting the result to the UI is a separate function.

GDScript 4 supports default arguments and return-type inference, but explicit types on public functions make refactor safe. Default arguments let callers omit optional parameters, so `draw(deck)` and `draw(deck, 5)` are both legal — convenient without overloads.

```gdscript
func draw(deck: Array, count: int = 1) -> Array:
    var drawn: Array = []
    for _ in range(count):
        drawn.append(deck.pop_back())
    return drawn
```

> [!WHY]
> Small, single-purpose functions compose into rules. `can_play` + `apply_penalty` + `advance_turn` read like a sentence and each can be tested in isolation. When a rule changes, you edit one function — not a 200-line `play_card` monolith.

Prefer pure functions (no side effects) for rule logic; reserve state mutation for clearly-named `apply_*` functions.

codeSnippets.caption: Two small functions: draw and can_play.

practicePrompt.instructions: Write a function `is_penalty_card(rank)` that returns true when rank is 2, 3, or 15 (Joker).
practicePrompt.solutionCode:
func is_penalty_card(rank: int) -> bool:
    return rank == 2 or rank == 3 or rank == 15

quizQuestions.prompt: What does the `->` arrow in a function signature specify?
quizQuestions.explanation: `func f() -> bool` declares that f returns a bool. Godot enforces this at runtime if you annotate it.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why prefer pure functions for game rules?
choices: They are testable in isolation and have no hidden side effects
quizQuestions.explanation: Pure functions depend only on their inputs and produce only a return value, so unit tests do not need to set up global state.

lessons.title: Arrays
lessons.bodyMarkdown:
# Arrays

An **array** is an ordered, indexed collection. In GDScript you declare one with `[]` and grow it with `append`, `pop_back`, `erase`, and so on.

A Kadi hand is naturally an array of cards; the draw pile is an array; the discard pile is an array. Mastering array methods is mastering half the game.

```gdscript
var hand: Array = []
hand.append({"suit": "Hearts", "rank": 7})
hand.append({"suit": "Clubs", "rank": 11})

var top_card: Dictionary = hand.pop_back()  # Jack of Clubs
var count: int = hand.size()  # 1
```

`pop_back()` removes and returns the last element — ideal for a stack-like draw pile. `pop_front()` and `push_front()` exist too but are O(n); avoid them in hot loops.

Iterate with `for card in hand:` or by index with `for i in range(hand.size()):`. Use `clear()` to empty a hand at round end.

> [!WHY]
> Arrays model ordered collections whose order matters. The discard pile's top card is `pile[-1]` (or `pile.back()`); the draw pile is LIFO. Picking the right structure — array vs dictionary vs set — saves you from off-by-one bugs and reshuffle disasters later.

Always check `size() > 0` before `pop_back()` — popping an empty array crashes.

codeSnippets.caption: Array operations on a Kadi hand.

practicePrompt.instructions: Create an empty array `discard_pile`, append a card dictionary for Ace of Spades (rank 14), then read the top card with `.back()`.

quizQuestions.prompt: Which method removes AND returns the last element of an array?
quizQuestions.explanation: `pop_back()` returns the last element and shrinks the array by one. `back()` reads without removing.

quizQuestions.prompt: What happens if you call `pop_back()` on an empty array?
quizQuestions.explanation: Godot raises an error: index out of bounds. Always guard with `if arr.size() > 0:` before popping.

lessons.title: Dictionaries
lessons.bodyMarkdown:
# Dictionaries

A **dictionary** maps keys to values. Declare one with `{}` and read with `dict[key]` or the safer `dict.get(key, default)`.

In Kadi we use dictionaries to model cards themselves (`{"suit": ..., "rank": ...}`) and to look up rules, like which ranks count as questions:

```gdscript
var PENALTY_VALUES: Dictionary = {
    2: 2,
    3: 3,
    15: 5  # Joker
}

func penalty_for(rank: int) -> int:
    return PENALTY_VALUES.get(rank, 0)
```

Keys can be any hashable type — ints, Strings, even enum values. Dictionaries do not preserve insertion order in Godot 4, so never rely on it for sequence; use an array when order matters.

`has(key)` tells you whether a key exists. Use it before reading when the key might be absent.

> [!WHY]
> Dictionaries replace long if/elif chains. Instead of branching on every rank to find its penalty, you look it up in O(1). Adding a new penalty card is a one-line table edit, not a code change — the data, not the control flow, encodes the rule.

When you find yourself writing `if rank == 2: ... elif rank == 3: ...`, ask whether a dictionary lookup would be clearer.

codeSnippets.caption: Dictionary lookup for penalty values plus a question check.

practicePrompt.instructions: Build a dictionary `SUIT_NAMES` mapping ints 0-3 to the strings "Hearts", "Diamonds", "Clubs", "Spades".
practicePrompt.hint: Keys are ints, values are Strings.

quizQuestions.prompt: What does `dict.get(key, default)` return when `key` is not present?
quizQuestions.explanation: `get` returns the supplied default instead of crashing, making it safer than `dict[key]` for optional keys.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why prefer a dictionary over a long if/elif chain for rank-to-value lookups?
choices: O(1) lookup and adding a card is a data edit, not a code change
quizQuestions.explanation: Dictionaries separate data from control flow, making rules table-readable and trivially extensible.

lessons.title: Classes and Objects
lessons.bodyMarkdown:
# Classes

A **class** bundles data and the functions that operate on it into one unit. In GDScript every script file is a class; you can also declare inner classes with `class_name`.

A Kadi card is a perfect candidate for a class:

```gdscript
class_name Card
extends RefCounted

var suit: String
var rank: int

func _init(s: String = "", r: int = 0) -> void:
    suit = s
    rank = r

func is_penalty() -> bool:
    return rank == 2 or rank == 3 or rank == 15
```

Classes give you **encapsulation**: the outside world calls `is_penalty()` without caring how rank maps to penalty. Change the internals later and callers keep working.

`extends RefCounted` means Godot frees the object automatically when nothing references it — perfect for short-lived cards. Use `extends Node` only when the object lives in the scene tree.

> [!WHY]
> Classes turn ad-hoc dictionaries into typed, behaviour-bearing objects. A `Card` knows whether it is a penalty; a `Player` knows its hand; a `Game` knows whose turn it is. Encapsulation localises change — when a rule shifts, you edit one class, not a web of free functions.

Prefer `class_name` so other scripts can `var c := Card.new("Hearts", 7)` without `preload`.

codeSnippets.code:
class_name Card
extends RefCounted

var suit: String
var rank: int

func _init(s: String = "", r: int = 0) -> void:
    suit = s
    rank = r

func is_penalty() -> bool:
    return rank == 2 or rank == 3 or rank == 15

func _to_string() -> String:
    return "%d of %s" % [rank, suit]
codeSnippets.caption: A Kadi Card class with constructor and helpers.

practicePrompt.instructions: Add a method `is_face()` to the Card class returning true for ranks 11-14.
practicePrompt.hint: Use a single `or` chain or a range check.
practicePrompt.solutionCode:
func is_face() -> bool:
    return rank >= 11 and rank <= 14

quizQuestions.prompt: What does `extends RefCounted` guarantee about an object?
choices: Godot frees it automatically when no references remain
It lives in the scene tree
quizQuestions.explanation: RefCounted objects are garbage-collected by reference count, so you never manually `free()` them — ideal for transient cards.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why use `class_name Card` at the top of a script?
choices: It registers the type globally so other scripts can use `Card.new()` without preload
It is required to extend RefCounted
quizQuestions.explanation: `class_name` exposes the type to the global namespace, removing the need for `preload("res://card.gd")` everywhere.

debugChallenge.bugDescription: The function only returns true when BOTH the suit and the rank match the top card. In Kadi a card is playable when it matches the suit OR the rank of the top card — so with this code almost nothing is playable and the game stalls.
debugChallenge.explanation: The boolean operator must be `or`, not `and`. `and` requires both conditions to hold (only the identical card would pass), while `or` correctly allows any card that shares the suit or the rank of the top card — the foundational Kadi play rule.
